name: Lyra
introduction: is the lyre of Orpheus, the musician of Greek myth whose songs could charm stones. It is a small constellation, a parallelogram of faint stars hanging from one of the brightest stars in the sky, Vega. High overhead on northern summer evenings, Vega is the brightest corner of the Summer Triangle.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Vega has a special place in astronomy. It was long used as the reference star for brightness, defining magnitude zero. In 1850, it became the first star after the Sun to be photographed, and in 1872 the first to have its spectrum photographed.

In 1983, the IRAS satellite found that Vega glows in infrared light from a disk of dust around it, the first such debris disk discovered. Disks like this are leftovers of planet formation, much like the Kuiper Belt in our Solar System.
Vega spins so fast that it bulges at the equator. We see it almost pole-on, so its hot poles face us. In about 12,000 years, Earth’s wobbling axis will make it the North Star.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Vega](hip:91262) is just 25 light-years away, a white star about twice the Sun’s mass and forty times as luminous.

[Sheliak](hip:92420) is a stellar wrestling match: two stars so close together that one pulls gas off the other, distorting both into egg shapes. Their combined brightness changes continuously every 12.9 days, and the star is the prototype of a whole class of eclipsing binaries. [Sulafat](hip:93194) completes the bottom of the lyre.

Near Vega, sharp eyes can split Epsilon Lyrae into two stars; a telescope reveals that each of them is double again, the famous “Double Double”. [Zeta¹ Lyrae](hip:91971) and [Delta² Lyrae](hip:92791) mark the corners of the parallelogram.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Halfway between Sheliak and Sulafat lies the Ring Nebula, M57, the glowing shell of gas shed by a dying Sun-like star. RR Lyrae, a faint star in Lyra, gives its name to pulsating stars that astronomers use as standard candles to measure distances to old star clusters. Each April, the Lyrid meteor shower, among the oldest recorded, with observations dating back to 687 BC, radiates from near Vega.
